questions.q: What is the correct order for a basic CLI resource lifecycle in this lesson?
options: Create the resource group, create the resource inside it, list what exists, delete the group
Delete the resource group, create the resource, create the group
Create the resource first, then create a resource group around it afterward
There is no meaningful order; az commands can run in any sequence
questions.explain: The resource group is created first as the container, then the resource is created inside it, then it's inspected, then the whole group is deleted.

questions.q: In `az vm create --image Ubuntu2204 --generate-ssh-keys`, what does --generate-ssh-keys do?
options: Creates a new local SSH key pair for authentication if one doesn't already exist
Picks the VM's size instead of its image
Deletes any existing SSH keys on the machine
Has no effect unless --admin-username is omitted
questions.explain: --generate-ssh-keys tells the CLI to generate a new SSH key pair locally when one isn't already present, instead of requiring a password.

questions.q: Why would you run `az resource list` instead of `az vm list` to check what's in a resource group?
options: az resource list shows every resource type in the group, not just VMs
az vm list is faster but returns incomplete VM data
az resource list only works with --output json
They return identical results in every case
questions.explain: az vm list only shows virtual machines; az resource list shows every resource type, including the disk, NIC, and public IP that az vm create also provisioned.

questions.q: What does --no-wait do on `az group delete --name rg-cli-demo --yes --no-wait`?
options: Returns control immediately instead of blocking the terminal until deletion finishes
Skips deleting resources that take longer than 30 seconds
Prevents the resource group from actually being deleted
Forces the command to run twice for confirmation
questions.explain: --no-wait lets the long-running delete operation continue in the background while you get your terminal back right away.

questions.q: Why is deleting the resource group the right cleanup step instead of deleting each resource individually?
options: One delete command removes every resource inside the group at once, instead of tracking down each piece by hand
Individual resources cannot be deleted under any circumstances
Deleting a resource group only removes its name, not its contents
az group delete is the only command capable of removing a virtual machine
questions.explain: A resource group is the blast-radius boundary — deleting it removes every resource inside it in one call instead of a scavenger hunt through disks, NICs, and public IPs.
